transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): All right kicking off, uh, thanks everyone for joining. Quick roll call. Samir from Redwood here. Lena and Marcus are on from eng.
[00:08] Aisha (NovaPay): Hi all, Aisha here. Tom and Priya are with me, and Liam will join in a few.
[00:14] Lena (Redwood): Morning.
[00:16] Tom (NovaPay): Morning.
[00:20] Samir: Cool. Agenda — quick perf recap, look at TTFT numbers with streaming enabled, kernel permutations Lena ran, then next steps.
[00:30] Samir: Lena, do you want to start with the TTFT numbers you pulled?
[00:35] Lena: Yeah sure. So to remind folks TTFT is time to first token, important for chat UX. We ran the new streaming patch on the staging cluster; results are fairly consistent with the bench we ran last week. Baseline without streaming was a median of around 240ms and 99th at nearly 760ms for the 2k token model variant with our sample traces. With streaming on and early token flushes enabled median dropped to ~130ms and 99th to ~420ms.
[01:05] Aisha: Wait 130ms median, is that cold-start or warm?
[01:08] Lena: Warm. Cold-starts are still higher — around 400–700ms depending on KV cache warmness. We also saw that enabling prefix KV caching for repeating user prompts knocked down cold-starts by about 40%.
[01:24] Tom: Can you explain the prefix caching behavior again? We have a lot of repeated payment prompt prefixes in NovaPay where the user intent is the same.
[01:30] Lena: Sure. Prefix caching stores the KV cache for a repeated prefix across requests so the runtime doesn't re-compute past attention keys. For NovaPay that helps because a lot of flows start with the same 3–4 tokens — the model can then start generation using already computed KV which reduces the first token compute.
[01:48] Priya: Is that safe for privacy? We need to make sure user PII isn't cached or persisted beyond TTL.
[01:54] Marcus: Good call. The cache is ephemeral and subject to TTL and scope rules in the POC config. We can set per-route TTL and also disable caching for routes flagged as sensitive. We'll send the exact config snippet after the call.
[02:05] Liam: Joining now, sorry I'm late.
[02:07] Samir: No worries. Next — kernel choices. Lena you tried the fused attention kernel vs the memory-optimized variant? What did we see?
[02:15] Lena: Yes. On the same hardware (A100-ish class in dedicated staging) the fused attention kernel gave better median latency for shorter sequences — so under 256 tokens median improved ~10–15%. But for longer sequences and 99th percentile the memory-optimized kernel was more stable. So it's basically a tradeoff: fused is fastest for common short chats, memory-optimized gives better tail at long sequences.
[02:41] Aisha: For our workload most sequences are under 128 tokens but we do have a 5% tail that hits 1k tokens during dispute flows.
[02:49] Lena: In that case our recommendation was to route by policy: default fused attention to hit your median SLO, and route the long-sequence traffic to memory-optimized variant or a fallback that has more memory headroom. We can do that with smart routing rules in the POC config.
[03:05] Tom: Does that require running two separate model variants or can it be done on the same model binary with different kernel flags?
[03:11] Marcus: It's possible both ways. We can keep one model and change runtime kernels at runtime for a request, but there is some setup cost when switching kernels — warmup and kernel-specific memory layouts. Practically we usually run two compatible variants pinned to different node pools, which gives predictable throughput.
[03:26] Aisha: How big is the memory/infra delta if we run both? What's the cost hit?
[03:31] Lena: Running both increases GPU capacity requirements — roughly +20–30% in reserved GPU compared to a single-variant optimized for median. But if you route only 5% of traffic to the memory-optimized pool the effective cost increase is closer to single-digit percent after autoscaling. We can model this in the perf spreadsheet.
[03:48] Priya: About streaming — what's the degradation in output quality or token ordering? We worry about truncated outputs or partial reasons.
[03:55] Lena: We didn't observe quality regressions in the sampled evals. Streaming flushes tokens earlier but the model's internal generation is the same. However, if you aggressively flush too early you can see more frequent short partial answers for prompts that require longer reasoning. So there's a knob there. We recommend enabling streaming for interactive routes, and non-streaming for long-form generation like dispute explanations.
[04:19] Aisha: Can we do hybrid? Start streaming and then switch to non-stream for specific prompts?
[04:24] Marcus: Yes, route-level flags can toggle streaming. We can also do per-request hints.
[04:29] Samir: I wanted to call out a practical note — our SDK has a streaming flag that flips on the runtime behavior and we capture TTFT metrics separately in tracing so you can quantify UX impact. We'll send the tracing dashboard link.
[04:40] Tom: Cool. Any kernel-level logs we can get? Our infra folks would like some low-level profiling.
[04:45] Lena: We generated kernel perf dumps and flamegraphs. The logs show the fused kernels spend less time in attention computation for short sequences, but they spike for the long tail when memory thrashing happens. I'll attach the perf logs to the spreadsheet.
[04:59] Liam: On the routing rules, how complex can we get? We need route rules that are cognizant of customer tier, region, and also model variant.
[05:06] Marcus: The routing engine supports composite policies — you can do region + model + latency budget + customer tier. It will evaluate policy predicates and route accordingly, including fallbacks if a pool is saturated.
[05:18] Aisha: We have strict SLAs on fraud flows — those need to be within 800ms 99p. Can Redwood meet that on hosted or dedicated?
[05:26] Lena: On dedicated with memory-optimized kernel and pinned capacity we are hitting ~500–600ms 99p for similar workloads in our benchmarks. On hosted multi-tenant, we usually advise the dedicated pool for SLA-backed flows.
[05:37] Tom: Any specific CPU/GPU packaging that helps us? We run on GCP and want to keep to our procurement.
[05:43] Marcus: A100/Tr4 class have good perf. On GCP the 80GB A100-equivalent or H100 variants give headroom for long sequences. We'll attach suggested instance types and node pools for your cluster.
[05:56] Samir: Ok let's jump to the new runs from this week — the 99th percentile delta after enabling KV cache and streaming combined. Lena?
[06:02] Lena: With both enabled we saw the 99th drop from ~760 to ~360 for the common 2k variant. For the 1k sequences the 99th moved from ~620 to ~310. Middle percentiles improved similarly. Important caveat: these were warm runs with steady traffic; cold starts still hit higher numbers.
[06:25] Aisha: Cold starts — what's the mitigation strategy? We can't have users wait 700ms during peak.
[06:30] Lena: A couple approaches: keep a small warm pool for low-latency-critical routes, increase prefix caching prewarm for likely prefixes, or use a short request coalescer that holds first few ms to batch micro-requests. Each has tradeoffs in cost and added latency for the earliest requests.
[06:46] Tom: That coalescer — sounds like added head-of-line latency. Do devs see more variability?
[06:51] Lena: If misconfigured yes; it's more useful for workloads with many very short requests where batching gives much better throughput at minimal added latency. We'll show you examples in the spreadsheet.
[07:01] Priya: Regarding security/compliance — last week we asked about audit logs for kernel and runtime changes. Any updates?
[07:08] Marcus: Audit logging for runtime flags and routing decisions is available. We record policy changes, kernel switches, and who/when. These logs are sent to your S3 bucket or custom endpoint and are tagged with request ids for traceability.
[07:22] Aisha: Good. Also SSO/SAML integration — is that ready for Dedicated?
[07:27] Samir: Yes, Dedicated supports SAML/SCIM SSO and RBAC. We'll share the guide.
[07:33] Liam: Aisha — our legal asked for a runbook showing behavior under OOM or GPU preemption; can Redwood provide a resilience doc?
[07:41] Samir: Yes we have a graceful degradation doc — fallback to smaller model, route to other region, and automatic retries with jitter. We'll attach the runbook.
[07:50] Tom: One nit — we've seen occasional tokenization differences between the model build locally and the staging. Could that affect latency?
[07:58] Lena: Tokenization mismatch affects effective sequence length which in turn affects latency and KV size. We'll validate tokenizer hash and provide the exact tokenizer build we used.
[08:08] Aisha: Anything new on quantization? We considered int8 variants earlier.
[08:13] Lena: Quantization can reduce memory and improve throughput, but there's a slight hit on quality for some prompts. For NovaPay we recommend evaluating 4-bit/8-bit on a sample prompt set. We didn't include quantized runs in this week's TTFT numbers. Next week we can add quantization permutations.
[08:30] Samir: Action items recap — Samir will send spreadsheet and tracing dashboard, Lena will run kernel permutations and quantization A/B, Tom to share traces, Priya to provide access.
[08:40] Aisha: Sounds good. If the numbers hold we want to do an on-site benchmark and maybe sign up for a small Dedicated pool pilot.
[08:48] Marcus: Great. We'll prepare a one-page recommendation that maps routing and kernel choices to cost delta and SLOs.
[08:55] Liam: One more question — fallbacks on region outage, how long to failover?
[09:00] Marcus: Typically a few seconds for routing fallback, but workload warm-up to reach steady-state can take a couple minutes. We'll run a failover simulation in the benchmark.
[09:10] Samir: Ok let's wrap. Anything else?
[09:13] Tom: Nope. Thanks all.
[09:15] Samir: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and the perf artifacts.
[09:18] Aisha: Thanks.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings; speaker labels were cleaned up where possible. Links referenced during the call: perf spreadsheet (link shared afterwards), streaming SDK docs (link), kernel perf logs (attachment).
